content: Umbilical venous catheters are frequently utilized during the neonatal period to establish vascular access. These catheters are inserted through the umbilicus and follow a specific anatomical path: they traverse the umbilical vein, the left portal vein, the ductus venosus, the middle or left hepatic vein, and the inferior vena cava, ultimately reaching the junction of the inferior vena cava and the right atrium. In contrast, umbilical artery catheters, which are typically paired and bilateral, initially course caudally to enter the right and left iliac arteries. This anatomical distinction allows for easy differentiation between umbilical venous and arterial catheters on abdominal radiographs. The umbilical venous catheter generally follows an anterior and cephalad trajectory along the midline umbilical vein before being directed posteriorly within the liver. Conversely, the umbilical artery catheter initially courses caudally and posteriorly to enter either the right or left iliac artery, then ascends superiorly within the more posteriorly located aorta. The optimal placement of the umbilical venous catheter tip is in the cephalad portion of the inferior vena cava or at the junction of the inferior vena cava and the right atrium. Anomalous positioning of the umbilical venous catheter is a common occurrence, primarily because the catheter is often inserted by pediatricians without the use of imaging guidance. If the catheter follows its normal course to the inferior vena cava or right atrium but is advanced excessively, it may extend through a patent foramen ovale or an atrial septal defect into the left atrium. If advanced further, it could enter a pulmonary vein. Alternatively, the catheter may continue through the right atrium into the superior vena cava or cross the tricuspid valve to enter the right ventricle. In some cases, the catheter may extend into the main pulmonary artery or its right or left branches. If the catheter reaches the left portal vein but does not proceed into the ductus venosus, it may deviate leftward into the more peripheral branches of the left portal vein. Alternatively, it may course rightward into the right portal vein or even flow hepatofugally into the main portal vein. In extreme cases, the catheter may extend further into the vessels that converge to form the portal vein, such as the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. Complications associated with umbilical venous catheters include the potential for perforation of an intrahepatic vascular wall, which can result in the formation of a hepatic hematoma. Additionally, intravascular thrombi may develop along the catheter's course. The catheter may also perforate the wall of the right or left atrium, leading to its entry into the pericardial space.
